title: 115 Spectral sensing to monitor nutrient concentrations in mixed-grass hay
content:
Abstract
The potential for continuous, on-animal forage quality monitoring remains largely unexplored, particularly with spectral sensing technology. This study evaluated a hand-held spectral sensing device to estimate nutrient composition of mixed-grass hay. A secondary objective was to test the sensor for on-animal use to monitor hay composition during consumption. Nutrient composition metrics included dry matter (DM), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent fiber (ADF), and crude protein (CP). From January to April, the sensor was used to scan10 mixed-grass round hay bales weekly, and grab samples were collected immediately after for wet chemistry analysis. The sensor measured reflectance at 18 wavelengths and distance using Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR). Readings were collected over 10 seconds at 1 hertz and were used to form the 19 primary features of a random forest regression. Data were split into three parts for analysis: 15% for hyperparameter tuning, 55% for training, and 30% for evaluation. Models produced root mean square prediction errors (RMSPE; % mean) of 9.49% (DM), 5.85% (NDF), 8.05% (ADF), and 22.8% (CP) compared to wet chemistry results. For on-animal testing, the sensors were mounted on halters worn by horses consuming hay. Sensor predicted hay composition was compared to grab samples collected from the area of the bale where the animal was eating. Although a small dataset, the halter-mounted spectral sensing system showed promise in accurately estimating forage composition, yielding RMSPEs of 8.02% (DM), 5.07% (NDF), 4.52% (ADF), and 23.5% (CP). The on-animal sensor system requires development, and future work should collect more extensive data on grazing animals, and across a wider range of forage composition.
